Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test simply opens a ZipFile on a known ZIP64 test archive (“COMPRESS-228.zip”) and expects no exception. The current issue report matches the observed failure: opening a valid ZIP64 file throws a ZipException with the message “central directory zip64 extended information extra field's length doesn't match central directory data. Expected length 16 but is 28”.

How the failure occurs step-by-step:
- ZipFile(File) delegates to ZipFile(File, String, boolean) which immediately calls populateFromCentralDirectory().
- populateFromCentralDirectory() locates the end of central directory (ZIP64-aware via positionAtCentralDirectory/positionAtCentralDirectory64 or 32) and then loops over central directory headers, invoking readCentralDirectoryEntry(...) for each entry.
- When readCentralDirectoryEntry(...) parses the central file header, it reads the extra field block and dispatches to the per-field parsers. For the ZIP64 extended information extra field (header ID 0x0001), the corresponding parser (Zip64ExtendedInformationExtraField.parseFromCentralDirectoryData or equivalent) validates the field’s length against what it infers from the central directory header.
  - The code determines which 64-bit values must be present (uncompressed size, compressed size, relative header offset, disk start) based on which corresponding 32-bit fields in the central directory are set to 0xFFFFFFFF.
  - From that, it computes an “expected” length (for example, 16 bytes if only the two sizes are needed).
  - In the provided archive, the ZIP64 extra field contains more data than strictly required by those indicators (e.g., it also includes the relative header offset and/or disk start), totaling 28 bytes. This is valid per the ZIP64 specification and accepted by other tools (zip -T passes).
  - The current implementation is overly strict: if the actual ZIP64 extra field length differs from the computed “expected” length, it throws a ZipException rather than ignoring additional bytes or parsing what is present.
- As a result, while reading the central directory of COMPRESS-228.zip, the parser encounters a ZIP64 extra field whose length exceeds the computed expectation and throws the exact ZipException seen in the issue report and test failure.

Root cause:
Overly strict validation in the ZIP64 extended information extra field parsing for central directory entries. The parser rejects ZIP64 extra fields that legitimately contain more data than the minimal set implied by the central directory header fields, instead of accepting the extra data and either parsing it or skipping it.

Impact:
Valid ZIP64 archives produced by some tools (e.g., DotNetZip with always-ZIP64 option) may include additional ZIP64 data in the central directory extra field. The current implementation throws an exception when encountering such files, preventing ZipFile from being opened.

Expected resolution direction:
Relax the length check in the ZIP64 extra field parsing for central directory data:
- Parse the required values inferred from the central directory fields.
- Accept longer-than-expected lengths by consuming only the required bytes and ignoring any trailing data (or parsing additional present fields if desired), rather than throwing an exception.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
